extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in mathematics studying topology/real analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and proof techniques about product topologies, the Tychonoff Product Theorem, nets/subnets, compactness characterizations, and quotient topologies. Focused on understanding and proving properties of products, convergence, and quotient constructions in general topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product topology (weakest making projections continuous)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a nonempty set and X_s is a topological space for each s in S, then the product X = ×_s X_s is given the weakest topology that makes each coordinate projection p_s : X → X_s continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This topology is characterized by the requirement that for each open U_s ⊆ X_s, the preimage p_s^{-1}(U_s) must be open in X. Use this universal/definitional property when checking continuity into/from a product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base for the product topology (finite-coordinate basic opens)
rubrics_metrics.description: A base for the product topology consists of finite intersections of sets of the form p_s^{-1}(U_s) where U_s is open in X_s; equivalently basic open sets are U_{s1} × ... × U_{sn} × ∏_{s not in {s1..sn}} X_s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only finite intersections (not infinite) are required to form the basic open neighborhoods. Use these basic opens to reason about openness, local structure, and finite-coordinate restrictions (e.g., visualizing function graphs on [0,1]^S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product topology = topology of pointwise convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: A net (or sequence) x_α in the product X converges to x if and only if p_s(x_α) → p_s(x) in X_s for each s in S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 10.35: use coordinatewise convergence to check convergence in the product. Combined with characterization of closed sets via nets, this simplifies checking closedness of subspaces of products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff
rubrics_metrics.description: If each X_s is Hausdorff, then the product X = ×_s X_s (with the product topology) is Hausdorff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: given distinct f,g in X, find s with f(s) ≠ g(s), choose disjoint open sets U_s and V_s in X_s separating coordinates, then p_s^{-1}(U_s) and p_s^{-1}(V_s) are disjoint open sets in X separating f and g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tychonoff Product Theorem (compactness of product)
rubrics_metrics.description: The topological product of compact topological spaces is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fundamental theorem often proved using Zorn's Lemma (equivalently the Axiom of Choice). Remarks emphasize its role as a generalization of diagonal/compactness arguments (e.g., Hilbert cube, Cantor diagonal process) and its central importance in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Zorn's Lemma / Axiom of Choice in Tychonoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs of the general Tychonoff theorem make explicit use of Zorn's Lemma (one form of the Axiom of Choice), both to guarantee nonemptiness of the product and to construct certain maximal covers/elements used in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the Axiom of Choice appears in multiple places in the argument (existence of choice functions/nonempty product, maximal covers). For countable products ([0,1]^∞) one can give a metric/diagonal subsequence proof avoiding the full generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert-cube metric yields product topology for countable products
rubrics_metrics.description: On X = ∏_{n=1}^∞ [0,1], the metric d(x,y) = Σ 2^{-n} |x_n - y_n| (Hilbert-cube metric) induces the product topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 10.28 gives a general result using a sequence of pseudometrics and Corollary 10.29 applies it to the Hilbert cube: show metric-open balls contain product-basic neighborhoods and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences are insufficient in general topological spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: In general topological spaces, sequences may fail to characterize limit points, closedness, or uniqueness of limits; examples show sequences can converge to multiple points or fail to detect closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two illustrative examples: cofinite topology on ℕ where a sequence can converge to every point, and a specially defined topology on integer-lattice points with (0,0) having no countable local base. Use these to motivate nets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of directed set and net
rubrics_metrics.description: A directed set D is a partially ordered set such that for any α, β in D there exists γ with α ≤ γ and β ≤ γ. A net in X is a function from a directed set D into X; notation x_α (α∈D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include positive integers (sequences), finite subsets of S ordered by inclusion, neighborhoods of a point ordered by reverse inclusion, and product-directed sets. Directedness allows simultaneously satisfying finitely many conditions on a net.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of a net (eventually / frequently)
rubrics_metrics.description: A net x_α converges to x_0 if for every neighborhood U of x_0 there is α_0 with α ≥ α_0 implying x_α ∈ U (the net is eventually in every neighborhood). The net is 'frequently in' E if for every α there exists β ≥ α with x_β ∈ E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negation: 'not eventually in E' means 'frequently in E^c'. Use 'eventually' to generalize sequence-based epsilon/N arguments and to handle finitely many simultaneous requirements via directedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nets characterize Hausdorff property (uniqueness of limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological space X is Hausdorff iff every convergent net in X has only one limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 10.31: proof uses disjoint neighborhoods for distinct limits to contradict eventual membership. Conversely construct nets converging to two points in non-Hausdorff spaces via neighborhoods directed set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nets characterize limit points and closed sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For any subset A and limit point x_0 of A there exists a net in A converging to x_0; a subset F is closed iff every convergent net in F has its limits in F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions 10.32 and Corollary 10.33: construct nets from neighborhoods or finite-intersection families to witness limit points; use these characterizations to replace sequence-based closure tests in general spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity characterized by nets
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : X → Y is continuous at x_0 iff for every net x_α → x_0 in X we have f(x_α) → f(x_0) in Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 10.34: use the net definition to check continuity without presuming Y is Hausdorff (but beware: if Y is not Hausdorff, images of convergent nets may have multiple limits and one must interpret the statement accordingly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of subnets (cofinal maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subnet x_{α∘μ} is obtained from a map μ : E → D (E directed) that is cofinal: for any β in D there exists γ in E with β ≤ μ(γ). The composition α∘μ is then a subnet of α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general notion (not just subset inclusion) is necessary to obtain the characterization of compactness via subnets. Subsequences are the prototypical example when D = E = ℕ and μ is increasing integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal nets and existence of universal subnets
rubrics_metrics.description: A net is universal if for every subset A of X the net is eventually in A or eventually in A^c. Proposition 10.36: every net has a universal subnet (proof uses Zorn's Lemma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal subnets are used in equivalences characterizing compactness. Construction proceeds by maximal families closed under finite intersections with the 'frequently in' property and then forming a directed product C×D for the subnet indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizations of compactness via nets
rubrics_metrics.description: For a topological space X the following are equivalent: (a) X is compact; (b) every universal net in X is convergent; (c) every net in X has a convergent subnet (Proposition 10.37).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: (a)⇒(b) via contradiction and finite subcovers; (b)⇒(c) uses existence of universal subnet; (c)⇒(a) construct a net from an open cover with no finite subcover to witness noncompactness. Use these equivalences to reprove Tychonoff via nets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second proof of Tychonoff via nets
rubrics_metrics.description: Use universal nets: a universal net in the product projects to universal nets in each factor, which by compactness converge; coordinate limits assemble to a product point that is the limit of the original net, proving compactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proof uses the characterization of compactness by nets (Prop. 10.37) and Proposition 10.35 (coordinatewise convergence). It avoids the maximal-cover/Zorn construction used in the first proof but still relies on Zorn's Lemma for universal subnet existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient topology (definition via quotient map)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ~ is an equivalence relation on X and q : X → X/~ is the quotient map, then the quotient topology is defined so that U ⊆ X/~ is open iff q^{-1}(U) is open in X; this is the finest topology on X/~ making q continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to check openness/continuity and to reason about maps factoring through quotients via the universal mapping property (Proposition 10.38).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal mapping property of quotient spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: If F : X → Y is continuous and constant on equivalence classes (x1 ~ x2 ⇒ F(x1)=F(x2)), then there exists a unique continuous map f : X/~ → Y with F = f∘q. Conversely, a continuous surjection q' : X → Z satisfying corresponding properties yields Z homeomorphic to X/~ (Prop. 10.38b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to recognize a space as a quotient: if q' is continuous onto Z and x1~x2 implies q'(x1)=q'(x2), and vice versa, then Z ≅ X/~. Corollary 10.39 adds that if F is also open, then the induced map is a homeomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projections as open maps and coordinate spaces as quotients
rubrics_metrics.description: For product X = ×_s X_s, each projection p_s : X → X_s is an open map. Hence X_s can be regarded as the quotient of X by the relation x1 ~ x2 iff p_{s'}(x1)=p_{s'}(x2) for all s' ≠ s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: basic open sets in X map under p_s to either open sets in X_s or whole X_s depending on whether the coordinate appears among the finite factors; thus projections carry opens to opens. Use this to build quotient descriptions of coordinates.
